speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON COMMISSION REPORTS CONCERNING NATIONAL CAPITAL AND VOLUNTARY ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to table a document which sets out the government's position regarding Book V of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism. I should also like to say something about Book V, relating to the national capital, and Book VI, relating to voluntary associations.
All Canadians jl am sure agree that the nation's capital should reflect in so far as possible the spirit and aspirations of our country.
The report of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism deals with this question as far as language is concerned.
I am pleased that many of the bodies referred to by the royal commission have already been making plans or taken action with regard to language and cultural aspects of the national capital. The city of Ottawa announced its program with regard to bilingualism some months ago; more recently the province of Ontario has announced a plan regarding service to its public in Canada's two official languages; representatives of voluntary organizations, business and educational bodies and private citizens joined forces recently to form the Alliance for the Development of Bilingualism in the Canadian Capital Region for the purpose of co-ordinating activities and exchanging information.

The report which has been tabled sets out more fully the government's position with regard to those of the 17 recommendations addressed to the federal government. Briefly, the government accepts the first recommendation regarding the equality of the two official languages for federal purposes. This has already been formalized in legislation, the Official Languages Act. The government also intends to continue to pursue the direct and positive role which it has been pursuing in the Capital Region, which is the second of the Royal Commission's recommendations.
Recommendations 3 through 6 and Recommendation 14 relate to various services being provided in both languages. The government accepts these recommendations, with the reservation that Recommendation 4 concerning commissionaires, elevator operators, and other personnel
dealing with the public should be implemented progressively so as to avoid hardship for unilingual employees.
Recommendations 7 through 13 are addressed to Ontario and Quebec separately or jointly or to local governments in the Capital area.
The recommendations relate to public services in the two languages, the courts and new proposed jurisdictions for various school boards. Obviously these matters fall within the jurisdiction of the provinces or the municipalities concerned. Insofar as provincial and municipal services are concerned, the co-operation of the federal government has been sought and given in certain instances in the past. The government will examine most sympathetically further possibilities of helping in other appropriate ways, if provincial or municipal authorities concerned judge this to be useful.
Recommendation 15 deals with the integration of transport and communications within the Capital area. This question is already the subject of planning between the NCC and various local authorities; the same can be said of Recommendation 16 regarding government buildings to be constructed or rented in the Capital area on both sides of the Ottawa River.
Recommendation 17 proposes the establishment of a specific advisory tripartite agency to be charged with the responsibility for co-ordination of the overall programme for the Capital area, and which it is suggested, with the passage of time, might acquire new functions and stature.
The government considers that, in addition to its role in urban planning, the National Capital Commission is the logical body to co-ordinate, at the federal level, activities to extend bilingual capabilities and services in the National Capital Region. The role of the National Capital Commission will not alter the existing allocation of responsibilities within the federal administration for achieving goals with regard to official languages and cultural development. It will, however, add a new and desirable dimension by giving other levels of government within the National Capital Region a single channel through which to seek assistance and benefit from expertise in the federal sector.
One of the complicating factors in dealing with the National Capital is the multiplicity of jurisdictions involved. In addition to the federal and two provincial governments, local and regional governments, school boards, and other authorities are in themselves very numerous. Two conclusions are inescapable. No single government or authority can by itself build a truly national capital: success depends upon the will of many governments and especially of the people they represent to give themselves to the task of creating a capital worthy of the nation. Secondly, a continuing dialogue must be maintained to assure that energies are channeled in a common direction; that in seeking the goal we are pulling together,

December 22, 1971
Bilingualism and Biculturalism
not apart. This is the ultimate object of the government's policy outlined above.
I should now like to turn briefly to the last volume of the royal commission, Book VI relating to voluntary associations. Here the commission, while analysing in depth the many facets of associational life in Canada, makes no formal recommendations. One theme, which runs strongly throughout the whole of the report, is the importance of maintaining good communications between francophone and anglophone branches of Canadian associations and between the general membership of the two major language groups. The commissioners suggested that simultaneous interpretation at annual conferences or conventions would be a useful way to assure more effective communication. I am glad to say, Mr. Speaker, that the government has been operating a modest program of assistance in this area since the beginning of the current fiscal year. We have ascertained that there is, indeed, an active interest among associations with respect to this program. The government is giving continuing consideration to Volume VI of the royal commission report and looking carefully at their observations regarding the trend of developments in this important aspect of Canadian life. Should further programs of co-operation between associations and the government be developed in the area of language, Mr. Speaker, these will be announced.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON COMMISSION REPORTS CONCERNING NATIONAL CAPITAL AND VOLUNTARY ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I fully agree that, as the national capital, the Ottawa region should reflect the reality of Canada. For that reason the recommendations of Volume VI of the B and B report must certainly be treated with respect. I am also pleased to see the encouragement that the government is giving to voluntary associations in this area.
I am not going to deal in detail with the government's response to the recommendations concerning the national capital region as provided in the document the Prime Minister just tabled. He was courteous enough to send me a copy of it this morning. In many respects it represents simply a declaration of the obvious. It quite properly notes that several of the recommendations are addressed to other jurisdictions where the only thing the federal government can offer is help and encouragement. The federal government cannot direct in those areas and that, of course, is how it should be under our system of government.
The National Capital Commission of course has a valuable, indeed an essential, role to play in the national capital area. I think one should note in passing that its existence involves some diminution of funds available to the municipal units in the area and that this diminution perhaps impedes thosa municipal units from making progress as rapidly as they would like to.
I fully agree that co-operation is necessary at all levels of government, although I must say that I hope the episode relating to what I believe is now called the Portage bridge is not an example of the kind of co-operation the federal government intends to display in future in this area.
As to the recommendation of the Commission on the necessity of promoting in every respect the equality between Anglophones and Francophones in the national capital, we agree with the attitude of the government which proposes to increase its role in that field. However, we stress the importance of constant and close consultations in this regard between the federal government, on the one hand, and the Quebec and Ontario governments on the other, to ensure that neither of those two governments ever feels that its rights are being encroached upon by the decisions concerning the national capital.
Our common goal must be to ensure that the capital region is a reflection of the Canadian reality. That means, of course, recognition of the English and French facts. However, it also involves a recognition of the cultural diversity of our country that goes beyond English and French. There is no recommendation in this volume of the bilingualism and biculturalism report on this subject, but we should not discuss the issue of national unity without re-emphasizing the importance of Canadian pluralism.
We should also not forget that in terms of government action we are discussing bilingualism in an institutional rather than in a personal sense. In Ottawa, as in Canada as a whole, there must be recognition of the fact that the majority of Canadians, whether they are English-speaking or French-speaking, are not bilingual. There must be acceptance of the fact of unilingualism as well, and that applies equally to French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians. The worst way to encourage bilingualism would be to try to enforce it too rigidly. There are areas where individual bilingualism is, in principle, essential. There can be do doubt about that. However, we cannot expect to correct everything overnight. There must be no injustices to older people who grew up in a different era. That, too, would be doing a disservice to the bilingualism it is desired to develop.
What we are working for, and what the commission I am sure was working for in preparing this report, is a country, and in this specific instance a capital region, where the individual Canadian can live in dignity and know that his language and origin will be respected, that he will be respected as an individual. If we remember that and apply it, we shall certainly be helping the cause of national unity.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON COMMISSION REPORTS CONCERNING NATIONAL CAPITAL AND VOLUNTARY ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity that I have to speak in French in the House. I know that I am not really ready to do so, but I feel that it is a fitting occasion and I will make a try.
We of the New Democratic Party are quite satisfied with the policy of the government which is endeavouring to implement the recommendations appearing in volume V of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism.
We sincerely hope that this policy will alter our national capital, so that it may become truly representative of the bilingual and multicultural facets of our country.
We think that it is exceedingly important that this action be immediately undertaken in order to consolidate the

December 22, 1971

already established bases so that our capital will be truly national.
It is very important that all Canadians, including French-speaking Canadians, feel they are really welcome in the capital.
French-speaking Canadians have had long-standing grievances about the Anglophone character of Ottawa.
We therefore believe it is urgent for the government to make already announced arrangements so that Ottawa can become the capital of all Canadians regardless of their racial origin, language and status.
In short, we claim for each and everyone the inalienable rights that are theirs.

For too long, Mr. Speaker, too many Canadians have felt themselves to be strangers in their own capital. For too long, for too many Canadians visiting their national capital was almost like visiting a foreign land. The situation was, and is, iniquitous and one of the factors generating tension within the nation. In accepting and implementing recommendations one and two in Book V of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism which deal with the equality of the French and English languages in the federal context and the provision of services in French and English, the government will be going a long way toward removing an ancient and completely justified grievance. I am pleased to see that in his remarks, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) recognized that in attempting to do this we also recognize that a great many people in this capital are not bilingual and that provision must be made for that fact.
We also welcome the suggestion that the federal government, in accordance with the recommendations of the royal commission, will be attempting to foster a greater integration of essential services, such as transportation-, on both sides of the Ottawa river, and that there are now also enhanced prospects of a more equitable distribution of new government construction on either side of the river.
For a long time I have been of the opinion that the boundaries of what is to constitute the capital of Canada should be extended beyond the city limits of Ottawa to coincide more directly with the boundaries of the national capital region as established in the National Capital Act of 1959. Such a capital would more closely reflect the make-up of this nation in terms of language, culture and of social organization, since it would include both urban and rural districts, than does our present capital. I am pleased to see that in accepting the recommendations of the royal commission the government is moving some distance in this direction.
The recommendations envisage the establishment of a tripartite committee of the three senior governments in the capital region, the federal government, the government of Ontario and the government of Quebec. Again, this is most welcome. It should mean more co-ordination of effort, less waste and greater equality of condition.
But here I should like to enter two caveats. First, I believe that the municipalities concerned must be represented on the committee in some formal way if many
Bilingualism and Biculturalism
potential difficulties are to be anticipated and misunderstanding is to be avoided. Second, the three senior governments would seem to have equal authority. Given the current political situation in the country, I can see no way around that particular approach, but it worries me because the capital is, after all, the capital of the whole nation and there might be a tendency for the provincial governments to be too strongly influenced by purely local concerns with the result that the national interest might sometimes be lost. As I say, I can offer no concrete suggestions to overcome this potential flaw but I raise the point in the hope that some attention will be devoted to it and some effort made to avoid the pitfalls.
As to the recommendation that federal government policy on the national capital be co-ordinated insofar as possible by one body at the federal level and that the National Capital Commission is the logical body to undertake that task, we in this party are in wholehearted agreement.
Finally, with respect to the Prime Minister's remarks concerning volume six, which deals with voluntary associations, we welcome the undertaking that the government will be giving the report continuing and careful consideration. I hope that in so doing the government will, in considering the French-English aspects of the question, consider seriously as well the value of voluntary associations in developing and defining the multicultural nature of our Canadian society and frame its eventual policies accordingly.
The national capital should be the jewel in the crown of our nation. In order to be so it must reflect the true character of our nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, everybody sincerely hopes for a national capital which would really reflect the existence of the various Canadian ethnical groups. However, this ideal capital which we all want requires understanding and co-operation from those living around it.
When we hear people complaining that the capital of Ottawa is not giving them their due, we must ask ourselves if they are ready to make the necessary sacrifices to benefit from it. They are ready to avail themselves of its

December 22, 1971
Regional Economic Expansion
advantages but are seldom willing to meet their obligations.
The statement of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is quite in order. Regarding bilinguism, we learned through the Commission's reports that French is spoken in Quebec and English in the other provinces. Everyone has known that for a long time.
The Commission's recommendations are far from being clear. Referring to Volume VI, the Prime Minister said and I quote:

Here the Commission, while analysing in depth the many facets of associational life in Canada, makes no formal recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, I believe we have the wrong approach to this problem if, for instance, we compel people of 40, 45 and even 50 years of age to learn a second language. To my mind this is abusing the good will of people. The Commission should recommend-and the government should follow suit-that a federal-provincial conference on education be held in order to look into the possibility of teaching the two languages right from the first school year across Canada.
If we took such action, in less than 10 years our country, including its capital, would become bilingual.
We should not attempt the impossible by forcing 40- or 50-year-old citizens to learn French or English. The right hon. Prime Minister did not wait until he was 52 to learn English; that is why he speaks it so well now, because he learned it in his youth, and he knows that. However, the Leader of the Official Opposition has trouble learning French because he started too late. That is a striking example, Mr. Speaker.
If the government suggested that the provinces-since education comes under provincial jurisdiction-finance their departments of education in order to have French and English taught in every school in Canada from the first year, we would not have to say this today: We want a bilingual capital, we want bilingualism, we want goodwill between English-speaking and French-speaking citizens. The whole country would be naturally bilingual, as a result of education.
That is the solution to the problem and that is my recommendation following the right hon. Prime Minister's statement.

speechtext: In view of the bilingual program in Canada, will the government consider the advisability of making all road signs on the Trans-Canada Highway and other federal roads bilingual?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. Jerome (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):

I am informed by the Department of Transport, the National Capital Commission and the Department of Public Works, as follows: At the present time the Federal Government is pursuing a policy of making all road signs on Federal roads bilingual. This policy is being acted on as quickly as practical. The road signs on the Trans-Canada Highway are the responsibility of the province through which the highway passes. All the provinces use the "Manual for Uniform Traffic Control Devices for Canada" as a guide and this manual supports the principles of symbolized and bilingual signs.
All road signs on NCC controlled parkways and driveways in the National Capital Region are bilingual. These signs are updated as required, as for instance when standard symbols replace written signs. As far as highway facilities under the Department of Public Works' jurisdiction are concerned, signing is generally in accordance with the provincial standards in which the facility is located.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, December 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacEachen (for the Minister of Finance) that Bill C-261, to amend the Customs Tariff, be read the second time and referred to the committee of the whole.

Mr. Speaker, while an examination of this bill would seem to indicate that the
December 22, 1971

changes being made are of a minor nature and not of any great significance, I feel that Bill C-261 is important in reflecting the failure of government policy to solve the problems of Canadian productivity. Instead of doing that, the government has introduced protective measures through a customs tariff change. I wish to refer to items 93902-3, 93902-42 and 93902-82 which deal with increasing the protection on plastics. If we look at some of these items in the bill, it is quite obvious what is happening in Canada. When discussing this matter in his opening remarks, the parliamentary secretary said something about bringing these items into line with other tariff items, but the effect is to increase the protection to an industry which, if it were properly organized, would not require this protection.
If we look at item 26910-1, while it is true the tariff for that particular section of feedstocks is being somewhat reduced from its previous level, nevertheless it seems rather inconsistent and certainly strange that in a country like Canada, with extensive mineral, oil and gas deposits, we should need any kind of protection at all on feedstocks. Some important feedstocks have arrived in the country at a low rate because they are the building blocks or primary materials used in the textile industry and other industries which give us our manufacturing base. To the extent that these raw materials are more expensive than they need be, it makes it more difficult for Canada to compete in the secondary manufacturing industry. Why is this so, Mr. Speaker? Why are we in this position when we have the raw materials? There is certainly an availability of capital. If anything, there has been too much capital poured into this industry rather than too little, yet we find ourselves in the position of requiring considerable protection for the products of the industry.
We have far too many plants serving the domestic market. There is considerable evidence to indicate that this is the case. The reason is that foreign ownership of this industry has, in many ways, aborted the possibility of this industry becoming efficient. Almost every major producer in the United States has established a branch plant in Canada of less than optimum size. This has split the market so badly that none can operate on any kind of an efficient scale.
An article by W. L. Dack in the August 21 edition of the Financial Post, headed "Trouble piles up for petrochemical firms", gives an example of the situation in Canada. I quote from this article:
For instance, the latest world-scale ethylene plants being built in the U.S. have a capacity of one billion pounds a year. But the entire Canadian ethylene market, which has just about reached that level, is being served by five domestic plants. All have unit costs running an estimated 205-25 per cent higher than those from these plants.
In the case of polyvinyl chloride monomer-the base material for one of the largest plastics groups-the unit cost of the worldscale plants can drop as much as 35-40 per cent below that of the smaller units.
"It's obvious that our big expansion splurge in petrochemicals was ill-timed."-
Over the years there has been encouragement given by the Canadian government to bringing investment into Canada without any real concern or thought as to whether that investment would, in fact, benefit the country. The argument was, the more the better. While on the surface it 24725-49
Customs Tariff Amendment Act, 1971
may have appeared we were providing competition by encouraging this multiplicity of plants, that kind of competition has, in fact, been of the worst kind. It has increased our costs away beyond what they should be and has prevented this country from effectively becoming a manufacturing nation on the scale it should be.
The argument is often used that one of the difficulties with our manufacturing industries in Canada is that we do not have access to larger markets, such as the United States for example, and that the problems in the petrochemical industry are related to the access to larger markets. As the article points out and other studies indicate, the Canadian market is more than adequate to have plants of a size and scale compared to the most efficient in the world, but we cannot afford the kind of splintering of the market that has taken place as the result of the numerous foreign owned plants being established in Canada. For over two years, the government has been conducting a study of the petrochemical industry to see what can be done to rationalize the industry. To date, no report has come from the government as to the results of that study.
While this has been going on, the industry is suffering, the consumer is suffering and the Canadian economy is suffering. We think the government has been remiss in trying to cover up its absence of policy by making tariff changes. While we are not opposed to these changes being made now, because we realize the industry does require an element of protection, we would not want to see a continuation of this approach. The government should be trying to face the issue in some more fundamental way. Unless we can eventually arrive at a point at which we can abolish all tariffs and institute free trade, the unity of this country is in jeopardy. For a long time we have heard rumblings of discontent from the west, from the prairie provinces and from British Columbia, directed against the level of tariffs afforded to the manufacturing and processing industries, while western producers must sell their products on a free market without protection. The ties of confederation have been strained considerably over the years because of our failure to make Canadian industry effective to the point at which it would not require tariff protection.
Those industries which remained largely under Canadian ownership were able to effect the transition from small plants to larger and more viable units of production, and to more satisfactory forms of organization suited to the Canadian economic climate, but where industry, particularly manufacturing industry, fell under foreign ownership this process did not take place. Many of the branch plants saw their first interest in serving the parent plant, the multinational corporation, rather than trying to effect re-organization within the Canadian economy.
When we talk about the ill effects of foreign ownership, it is not an emotional thing. It is the result of an analysis of what foreign ownership has done to large segments of the Canadian economy. Instead of increasing the wealth of Canada and improving the ability of this country to compete in international markets, foreign ownership, particularly in the chemical industry, has often led to a much lower standard of living than we have reason to expect. Therefore, while we see no alternative to supporting the tariff changes proposed by the government in the face of

December 22, 1971
Customs Tariff Amendment Act, 1971
the emergency situation confronting the chemical and plastic industries, we believe it is imperative that policies be developed immediately to ensure that this kind of tariff protection is not required and that our industries will be in a position to manage on their own in a free trade world.

speechtext:

The hon. member asked what macerated paper pads were-item 19947-1. Well, these are pads made of a thick

layer of loose, ground up newsprint secured between two sheets of kraft paper, and they are used in the packaging of fruit to prevent it being bruised in transit. This particular tariff change will be of principal benefit to the fruit growers of British Columbia.

There were objections to a reduction in duty on the part of Canadian refiners. The hon. member for Edmonton West emphasized last night the importance of the petrochemical industry in a neighbouring riding to his. The refining industry is also of considerable importance in the Edmonton district and this is a factor to be borne in mind. The next paragraph deals with machines and parts thereof, for use exclusively in logging, such operation to include the removal of the log from stump to skidway, log dump, or common or other carrier. This proviso, which I understand is a new provision in this bill, removes these items from the application of the tariffs listed in the case of importation into Canada of any goods enumerated if the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, considers that it is in the public interest and that the goods are not available from production in Canada by allowing a remission of the duty specified in the item.

The types of products to which the hon. member is referring are subject to tariff items 42700. They are treated in the same way under that item as is proposed for logging equipment under this item. Mr. Chairman, I wish to make an inquiry about item 47825-1 which includes wheelchairs, walkers and other aids to locomotion. I have received a number of complaints concerning the importation from Switzerland of a mobile wheel chair for invalids of a type that is not
Customs Tariff Amendment Act, 1971
manufactured anywhere else, but the argument used by the department is that because there are other products available that will assist locomotion, the customs tariff must apply to this import. What is the reason for this? Very few of these wheelchairs will be imported from Switzerland. They are expensive. Why should this stipulation "of a class or kind made in Canada" apply in this case?
It seems to me that we should be prepared to remove this restriction. Because of disability, a person may find that this type of wheelchair suits him better than any other type. I understand the cost of such a wheel chair is $1,200 in Switzerland, and a 15 per cent tariff on top of that is a considerable amount of money. I note that there is no tariff applicable to hearing aids and parts for their repair. I believe the same situation should apply to invalid chairs.
I took up this matter with the officials and they were sympathetic, but they told me their hands were tied by this restriction concerning a class or kind made in Canada. The individual involved told me that he had discovered no suitable wheelchair for his use in Canada, that there were automatic wheelchairs and electric wheelchairs available in Canada but not of the type that he could operate. He had been to Switzerland and discovered a type there that suited him, but he was not able to import it because of the excessive cost to him that the 15 per cent tariff represented. I am sure that such cases seldom come to the attention of the department. Because of the nature of this item, because it has a personal application, there should be an exemption for it. But again this restricting phrase "of a class or kind made in Canada" governs the situation.
I can draw an analogy between this and an operation in a sawmill where people using milling machines are working with chip board. For the plastic veneer that they use in my area they tell me that the only suitable product comes from Germany. They laminate the chip board with it. There is another type of veneer manufactured in the United States, and several other kinds are manufactured in Canada, but there is a considerable difference in the type of product they can turn out using the stuff that they import from Germany. In a non-technical sense, these veneers look very much the same but they do not all perform the same function.
In the 14 years that I have been a member of this House, only one person has approached me seeking a concession with respect to tariff on an invalid chair. I am sure not more than 200 or 300 people throughout the country would be involved in this situation, and a concession should be made.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to convey my appreciation to the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney) for his participation in the debate on this bill. I wish to speak about certain changes that take place from time to time in the customs tariff. These changes are negotiated with other countries and when they are brought before Parliament they are fait accompli; there is no opportunity to change them. Under our present method of operating, changes to those agreements would involve changes to Ways and Means resolutions. It seems to me that hon. members should be in a better position, in cases where these negotiations have taken place, to bring about changes that, in their opinion, are advantageous or desirable in certain fields.
When on former occasions I have suggested that some items ought to be exempt, those exemptions were not granted. Several years later exactly the same kind of exemption as I suggested has been granted, often for the very same kind of product I had in mind. When I made my suggestion, there was no way of implementing it. The difficulty regarding our representations stems from the fact that we are remote from negotiations in which Canada discusses tariff changes say, under GATT, or the most favoured nation tariff. It seems to me that we need to learn something of what goes on in these discussions. At present, we must accept the entire change, or reject it. It is a case of all or nothing, and this leads to frustration.
Income Tax Amendment Law Act, 1971
However, I wish to congratulate the parliamentary secretary and the officials assisting him for the splendid job that was done in answering questions that I and other hon. members asked.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.
